title: HPV vaccination may protect against adverse pregnancy outcomes

analysis.time: The study was published on 2026-10-07. The data analyzed spans from 2006 to 2023.
analysis.location_and_population: The study was conducted in Sweden, focusing on singleton, first-time births among women aged 16-35 years.
analysis.event: A large Swedish study published in The BMJ found that HPV vaccination before pregnancy is associated with a lower risk of major pregnancy complications, including preterm birth. The researchers suggest that the benefits of HPV vaccination may extend beyond cancer prevention to reducing adverse pregnancy outcomes.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study included 624,713 singleton, first-time births, of whom 92,620 (15%) had received quadrivalent HPV vaccination before pregnancy. The findings showed statistically significant associations for preterm and very preterm birth, spontaneous preterm birth, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, and delivering a severely small baby. The risk reduction was more pronounced among women vaccinated before age 17.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study is observational, so no firm conclusions about cause and effect can be drawn. The authors acknowledge incomplete information on spontaneous abortions and limited investigation of the underlying clinical pathways. However, they state that the study minimized bias and misclassification, enabling assessment of both common and rare adverse pregnancy outcomes.

analysis.brief_en: A large Swedish study published in The BMJ on October 7, 2026, found that HPV vaccination before pregnancy is associated with a lower risk of major pregnancy complications, including preterm birth. The research, based on data from 624,713 singleton, first-time births among women aged 16-35 years in Sweden between 2006 and 2023, revealed that 15% of the participants had received quadrivalent HPV vaccination prior to pregnancy. The findings suggest that HPV vaccination may offer additional benefits beyond cancer prevention by reducing the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. The study highlights that the risk reduction was more significant among women vaccinated before age 17. However, the researchers emphasize that this observational study cannot establish a definitive cause-and-effect relationship, and they acknowledge limitations such as incomplete data on spontaneous abortions and unmeasured factors that could influence the results. Despite these uncertainties, the study's high-quality data and long follow-up period help minimize bias, supporting the safety and potential benefits of HPV vaccination during pregnancy.
